overview: A ball screw converts rotary motion into linear motion the same way a hobby lead-screw actuator does — a threaded rod turns and a nut travels along it — but with recirculating ball bearings riding in the thread groove instead of the nut's metal sliding directly against the screw. That single change is what makes it an industrial-tier part: rolling friction instead of sliding friction means far higher mechanical efficiency (often 90%+ vs. an Acme screw's 20-40%), and a preloaded ball nut removes almost all axial backlash, so commanding a specific position actually gets you that position, repeatably, move after move. It's driven externally by a stepper or servo motor coupled to the screw (it has no motor of its own), and because it's a precision mechanical component, it needs to be paired with a matching stepper/servo driver, limit switches to define safe travel, and usually a home sensor so the controller knows where zero actually is after every power-up.
simpleSummary: A precision screw-and-nut mechanism that turns a motor's spinning into smooth, accurate straight-line motion with almost no play, using ball bearings instead of a sliding nut.

specifications.leadPerRevolution: 1mm - 10mm per revolution (model-dependent, finer lead = more resolution, less speed)
specifications.maxLinearSpeed: Up to ~1 m/s on fine-lead high-speed screws, lower on high-force coarse screws
specifications.driveMotor: External NEMA23/NEMA24 stepper or AC/DC servo, coupled via a flexible shaft coupling
specifications.dutyCycle: Continuous duty at rated load (mechanically efficient, low self-heating compared to a sliding lead screw)

pinMap.name: MOTOR_A+
pinMap.function: Drive motor coil A terminal (bipolar stepper), energized in sequence with the other coil to rotate the screw.
pinMap.gotcha: This actuator has no onboard driver — it must be paired with an external stepper/servo driver sized for the motor's holding torque, not just its running current, since a ball screw under load can demand full torque at zero speed.

pinMap.name: MOTOR_A-
pinMap.function: Drive motor coil A other terminal.

pinMap.name: MOTOR_B-
pinMap.function: Drive motor coil B other terminal.
pinMap.gotcha: Swapping any one coil's two leads reverses rotation direction on that coil alone and desyncs the step sequence — if the carriage suddenly stalls or vibrates without moving, check for a single reversed lead before suspecting the driver.

pinMap.name: LIMIT_EXTEND
pinMap.function: Normally-open limit switch that trips when the carriage reaches full extension, used by the controller to stop or reverse the motor before the mechanism crashes into its hard stop.
pinMap.gotcha: Software-only travel limits are not a substitute for this switch — if the controller loses step count (stall, power glitch, EMI) it has no other way to know the carriage is about to hit the end block at full speed.

pinMap.name: LIMIT_RETRACT
pinMap.function: Normally-open limit switch that trips at full retraction.

pinMap.name: SWITCH_COMMON
pinMap.function: Shared common/return wire for the limit and home switches.

pinMap.name: HOME_SENSOR
pinMap.function: Dedicated home-position sensor (often a small optical or hall-effect flag), used at power-up to re-establish an absolute zero reference before any move.
pinMap.gotcha: Stepper-driven ball screws have no idea where they are after a power cycle — skipping the homing routine on startup and issuing an absolute move blind is a common way to slam the carriage into an end stop.

pinMap.name: ENCODER_A
pinMap.function: Optional motor-shaft quadrature encoder channel A, for closed-loop stall/position verification on servo-driven variants.
pinMap.gotcha: Only present on servo/closed-loop variants — a plain open-loop stepper version has no way to detect a missed step other than hitting a limit switch or home sensor unexpectedly.

pinMap.name: ENCODER_B
pinMap.function: Optional motor-shaft quadrature encoder channel B.

useCases.title: CNC or 3D-printer Z-axis
useCases.scenario: Drive a machine's vertical axis with a fine-lead ball screw for high positioning accuracy and near-zero backlash on layer height or cut depth.

useCases.title: Robotic linear stage
useCases.scenario: Provide a precise, repeatable single-axis slide for a pick-and-place mechanism or camera focus rail, homing to a known reference at every startup.

useCases.title: Heavy-load lift mechanism
useCases.scenario: Push/lift a load far heavier than a hobby linear actuator could manage, using the ball screw's high thrust rating and near-zero backlash to avoid sag under load.

useCases.title: Closed-loop servo positioning
useCases.scenario: Pair the servo-driven variant's shaft encoder with the driver's closed loop to detect and correct for any missed motion under unexpected load spikes.

useCases.title: End-of-travel safety interlock
useCases.scenario: Wire both limit switches into the motion controller's fault input so a stalled or runaway move stops the motor in hardware, independent of software travel limits.

commonlyPairedWith: NEMA 23/24 stepper motor or AC/DC servo
a4988-drv8825 / tb6600 stepper driver, or a servo drive
Linear rail / guide bearing for carriage support
oftenConfusedWith: linear-actuator (a self-contained hobby lead/Acme-screw actuator with its own integrated DC motor, no external driver needed, but noticeably more backlash and lower repeatability — this ball screw is a bare precision mechanism that needs an external motor and driver)
oftenUpgradedTo: Servo-driven ball screw with closed-loop encoder feedback, for stall detection and guaranteed positioning under variable load

beginnerMistakes: Treating it like a hobby linear actuator and expecting an integrated motor/driver — a bare ball screw needs an external stepper or servo motor and matching driver to do anything.
Skipping the homing routine after power-up and issuing an absolute-position move blind, risking a hard crash into the end stop.
Sizing the drive motor for running torque only, ignoring that a loaded ball screw can demand full holding torque even at a dead stop.
Relying on software travel limits alone with no physical limit switches wired in, leaving no hardware backstop if the controller loses step count.
Mounting the carriage load off-axis from the screw's centerline, inducing side-loading that accelerates ball-nut wear far faster than the rated life.
